prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistan's foreign ministry said Wednesday that it has lodged a "strong" protest with the U.S. ambassador over missile attacks conducted on Pakistani soil by unmanned drones. The aftermath of a suspected U.S. drone attack on a building in North Waziristan. The ministry said it summoned Ambassador Anne Patterson to underscore that such attacks violate Pakistan's sovereignty and should be stopped immediately. A statement from the ministry said Patterson was also told that the attacks have cost lives and undermined public support for Pakistan's counter terrorism efforts. The ministry lodged its protests three days after a missile strike from a suspected U.S. drone on a compound in South Waziristan killed 20 people. Pakistan has repeatedly raised objections to foreign nations violating its sovereignty to pursue terrorists. A U.S. ground operation in September that left several civilians dead rankled relations between the two countries. Last week, Pakistan's parliament passed a resolution that condemned any incursion on Pakistani soil by foreign forces. The resolution called for a review of the country's national security strategy and said the government needs to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The ministry said it handed Patterson a copy of the resolution. The U.S. and NATO, which have troops in Afghanistan, have been seeking a way to effectively battle militants who launch attacks from Pakistan's swath of tribal areas along the border. They have become frustrated with Islamabad over the years, saying it is not being proactive enough against militants -- a claim Pakistan denies. The United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from drones, which are controlled remotely. In another development, suspected Taliban militants kidnapped three government officials from an administrative office in Pakistan's tribal region Wednesday, officials said. The militants abducted two employees and a security guard from the Ambar district in Mohmand Agency. Mohmand is in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, where U.S. and Pakistani officials have reported a presence of militants. Earlier in the day, militants tried unsuccessfully to take control of a school in Mohmand and abduct about 100 students, authorities said. A shootout with Frontier Corps followed, in which one militant was killed and another arrested. The Frontier Corps is a paramilitary force which uses recruits from Pakistan's tribal areas and is overseen by Pakistani army officers. Also Wednesday, a suicide car bomber detonated explosives outside a police checkpoint in northwest Pakistan, killing two security personnel, officials said. The Wednesday afternoon attack in the Bannu district of the North West Frontier Province also wounded a dozen people, military sources said. The bomber targeted a check point near a military hospital, said the sources who did not want their names revealed because they are not authorized to speak to the media. CNN's Reza Sayah and journalist Janullah Hashimzada contributed to this report .

The protest followed the aftermath of a suspected U.S. drone strike on a building in North Waziristan. The ministry said it had summoned Ambassador Anne Patterson to emphasize that such attacks violate Pakistan’s sovereignty and must be stopped immediately.

In a statement, the ministry said Patterson was also told that the attacks had resulted in the loss of life and had undermined public support for Pakistan’s counterterrorism efforts.

The ministry lodged its protest three days after a missile strike by a suspected U.S. drone on a compound in South Waziristan killed 20 people.

Last week, Pakistan’s parliament passed a resolution condemning any incursion onto Pakistani soil by foreign forces. The resolution called for a review of the country’s national security strategy and said the government must safeguard Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. The ministry said it had handed Patterson a copy of the resolution.

The United States and NATO, which have troops in Afghanistan, have been seeking ways to more effectively combat militants who launch attacks from Pakistan’s tribal areas along the border. Over the years, they have grown frustrated with Islamabad, saying it has not been proactive enough against militants — a claim Pakistan denies.

The United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from remotely controlled drones.

In a separate development Wednesday, suspected Taliban militants kidnapped three government officials from an administrative office in Pakistan’s tribal region, officials said.

The militants abducted two employees and a security guard from the Ambar district in Mohmand Agency. Mohmand is part of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, where U.S. and Pakistani officials have reported a militant presence.

Earlier in the day, militants unsuccessfully attempted to seize control of a school in Mohmand and abduct about 100 students, authorities said. A shootout with the Frontier Corps followed, leaving one militant dead and another arrested.

The Frontier Corps is a paramilitary force that recruits from Pakistan’s tribal areas and is overseen by Pakistani army officers.

Also Wednesday, a suicide car bomber detonated explosives outside a police checkpoint in northwest Pakistan, killing two security personnel, officials said.

The Wednesday afternoon attack in the Bannu district of the North West Frontier Province also wounded a dozen people, military sources said. The bomber targeted a checkpoint near a military hospital, according to the sources, who did not want their names revealed because they are not authorized to speak to the media.

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry announced Wednesday that it had delivered a “strong” protest to the U.S. ambassador regarding missile strikes carried out by unmanned drones inside Pakistani territory.

The protest followed what was believed to be a U.S. drone strike on a building in North Waziristan. According to the ministry, Ambassador Anne Patterson was called in and told that such operations breach Pakistan’s sovereignty and must end at once.

In its statement, the ministry said Patterson was also informed that the attacks had caused deaths and weakened public backing for Pakistan’s counterterrorism campaign.

The formal complaint came three days after a missile fired by a suspected U.S. drone hit a compound in South Waziristan, killing 20 people.

Pakistan has often objected to foreign countries entering or attacking inside its territory in pursuit of terrorists. Relations between Pakistan and the United States were strained in September after a U.S. ground operation resulted in the deaths of several civilians.

The previous week, Pakistan’s parliament approved a resolution denouncing any entry by foreign forces onto Pakistani land. The measure also urged a reassessment of the nation’s security policy and said the government must protect Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial boundaries. The Foreign Ministry said it gave Patterson a copy of that resolution.

The United States and NATO, both of which have forces stationed in Afghanistan, have been looking for ways to more effectively confront militants who carry out attacks from Pakistan’s tribal belt along the Afghan border. Over the years, they have expressed frustration with Islamabad, arguing that Pakistan has not acted aggressively enough against militants — an accusation Pakistan rejects.

The United States is the only country active in the area known to have the ability to fire missiles from remotely piloted drones.

In a separate incident Wednesday, suspected Taliban militants seized three government workers from an administrative office in Pakistan’s tribal region, officials said. The gunmen took two employees and a security guard from the Ambar district of Mohmand Agency.

Mohmand lies within the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, where both U.S. and Pakistani officials have said militants are present.

Earlier Wednesday, authorities said militants attempted but failed to take over a school in Mohmand and kidnap roughly 100 students. A gunbattle with the Frontier Corps ensued, leaving one militant dead and another in custody.

The Frontier Corps is a paramilitary organization staffed with recruits from Pakistan’s tribal areas and commanded by officers from the Pakistani army.

Also on Wednesday, officials said a suicide attacker detonated a car bomb outside a police checkpoint in northwestern Pakistan, killing two security personnel.

Military sources said the afternoon bombing in Bannu district, located in the North West Frontier Province, also injured 12 people. The attacker struck a checkpoint near a military hospital, according to sources who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak with the media.

CNN’s Reza Sayah and journalist Janullah Hashimzada contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
**Pakistan protests suspected U.S. drone strikes in Waziristan amid militant violence**

**Islamabad, Pakistan (CNN)** — Pakistan lodged a strong protest with the U.S. ambassador after suspected American drone strikes targeted areas in the country’s northwestern tribal region of Waziristan, Pakistani officials said, as separate militant incidents were reported in Mohmand and Bannu.

Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the U.S. ambassador in Islamabad and conveyed what it described as “serious concern” over the strikes, saying they violated Pakistan’s sovereignty and risked fueling further instability in the region.

The suspected drone attacks reportedly took place in Waziristan, a mountainous area along the Afghan border that has long been used as a haven by militant groups, including factions linked to the Pakistani Taliban and al Qaeda. Pakistani security officials said the strikes targeted suspected militant compounds, though details on casualties could not be independently verified.

The United States rarely comments publicly on individual drone operations. U.S. officials have previously defended such strikes as a key counterterrorism tool against militant networks operating in remote border areas, while Pakistan has repeatedly condemned them as unlawful and counterproductive.

The diplomatic protest came as Pakistan faced additional violence in nearby regions.

In Mohmand, part of the former tribal belt, militants attacked security positions, according to local officials. Pakistani forces responded, and clashes continued for several hours. Authorities did not immediately release a full casualty count.

Separately, in Bannu, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, militants were reported to have targeted security personnel in an attack that heightened concerns about the deteriorating security situation in the northwest. Bannu has seen repeated militant activity in recent months, including assaults on police, military convoys and security installations.

Pakistan’s government has been under pressure to contain a resurgence of militant violence, much of it claimed by or attributed to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, an umbrella group ideologically aligned with the Afghan Taliban but organizationally separate from it.

Islamabad has accused militants of using sanctuaries across the border in Afghanistan to plan attacks inside Pakistan. Afghan Taliban authorities have denied allowing their territory to be used against neighboring countries.

The suspected drone strikes add another layer of tension to an already complex security environment. While Washington and Islamabad have cooperated for years on counterterrorism, drone attacks have remained deeply unpopular in Pakistan, where civilian leaders often denounce them publicly even as analysts say coordination has at times occurred behind the scenes.

Pakistani officials said the government reiterated to the U.S. ambassador that counterterrorism operations must respect Pakistan’s territorial integrity and that unilateral action undermines bilateral relations.

The incidents in Waziristan, Mohmand and Bannu underscore the continuing volatility along Pakistan’s western frontier, where militant violence, cross-border tensions and counterterrorism operations remain a persistent challenge for the government in Islamabad.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

Patterson on Monday to lodge a formal protest over recent drone missile strikes on Pakistani territory, saying the attacks violated the country’s sovereignty and risked undermining cooperation in the fight against militancy.

Foreign Ministry officials said Patterson was called to the ministry in Islamabad and handed a demarche expressing Pakistan’s “serious concern” over the strikes, which reportedly targeted suspected militant hideouts in the country’s tribal areas near the Afghan border. Pakistani officials said such operations, carried out without public authorization from Islamabad, were “unacceptable” and could inflame anti-American sentiment.

“The Government of Pakistan has consistently maintained that drone attacks inside Pakistani territory are a violation of sovereignty and territorial integrity,” a ministry official said. “They are counterproductive and complicate our efforts to build public support for counterterrorism operations.”

The United States has long viewed Pakistan’s border regions, particularly areas of North and South Waziristan, as sanctuaries for al-Qaida and Taliban-linked militants involved in attacks on U.S. and NATO forces in Afghanistan. Washington has rarely acknowledged specific drone operations, but U.S. officials have argued that militant networks operating from Pakistani soil pose a direct security threat.

Pakistan, while publicly condemning the strikes, has faced persistent pressure from Washington to do more against insurgent groups using the rugged frontier as a base. The issue has become one of the most sensitive points in U.S.-Pakistan relations, exposing a divide between American counterterrorism priorities and Pakistan’s insistence on sovereign control over military action within its borders.

The latest protest comes amid heightened tensions over civilian casualties and the political fallout from cross-border operations. Pakistani leaders have warned that drone strikes strengthen extremist narratives, erode trust between the allies, and place the government in a difficult position domestically.

Security analysts in Islamabad said the summoning of Ambassador Patterson reflected growing frustration within Pakistan’s civilian leadership, even as both countries continue intelligence and military cooperation against militant groups.

“The relationship is defined by mutual dependence and deep mistrust,” said one analyst. “Pakistan wants U.S. support, but it cannot ignore public anger over strikes seen as unilateral violations of national territory.”

The U.S. Embassy did not immediately issue a detailed response. American officials have previously emphasized the importance of continued cooperation with Pakistan in combating terrorism and stabilizing Afghanistan.

The dispute underscores the broader strain in the bilateral relationship: Pakistan says counterterrorism operations must respect its sovereignty, while the United States insists that militant sanctuaries along the Afghan border remain a critical threat. As both governments seek to balance security needs with political pressures, drone attacks are likely to remain a flashpoint in ties between Islamabad and Washington.

counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS: Pakistan Protests U.S. Drone Strikes After South Waziristan Attack Kills 20**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Pakistan has lodged a strong objection to continued U.S. drone attacks inside its territory after a missile strike in the tribal region of South Waziristan killed at least 20 people, intensifying an already tense debate over sovereignty, counterterrorism cooperation and rising Taliban violence along the Afghan border.

Pakistani officials condemned the strike as a violation of the country’s territorial integrity, saying such attacks undermine public support for the government and complicate efforts to confront militant groups operating in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas. The South Waziristan attack, reportedly carried out by an unmanned U.S. aircraft, targeted a suspected militant compound in an area long considered a stronghold for Taliban and al-Qaida-linked fighters.

The latest incident comes despite a resolution passed by Pakistan’s parliament calling for an end to foreign incursions and demanding that no outside power conduct military operations on Pakistani soil without Islamabad’s approval. Lawmakers have repeatedly argued that drone attacks inflame anti-American sentiment and strengthen militant propaganda, even when the strikes are aimed at high-value extremist targets.

Pakistan’s government has faced mounting pressure from opposition parties, religious leaders and tribal representatives to take a harder line against Washington. Critics say the strikes amount to unilateral military action inside Pakistan, while U.S. officials have historically defended drone operations as a necessary tool against militants planning attacks in Afghanistan and beyond.

The dispute is unfolding against a backdrop of escalating Taliban violence in Pakistan’s tribal areas. Militants have carried out attacks on security forces, government offices and rival tribal leaders, while also seeking to impose their authority in remote districts where the state’s presence is limited. South Waziristan in particular has seen repeated clashes involving Taliban factions, local fighters and Pakistani troops.

Security analysts say the Pakistani government is caught between competing pressures: the need to confront extremist networks responsible for deadly attacks across the country, and the political cost of appearing to tolerate U.S. military action within its borders.

“The drone issue has become a symbol of sovereignty for Pakistan,” one Islamabad-based analyst said. “Even when the targets are militants, the perception that another country can strike at will creates a major domestic backlash.”

Washington has not publicly confirmed responsibility for the South Waziristan strike, in keeping with its usual policy regarding drone operations in Pakistan’s border regions. But U.S. officials have privately maintained that militant sanctuaries in the tribal belt pose a direct threat to international forces in Afghanistan and to global security.

Pakistani leaders, meanwhile, say counterterrorism efforts must be conducted under Pakistani authority and in line with parliamentary directives. The government has warned that continued strikes could damage cooperation with the United States at a time when both countries are trying to coordinate policy in the region.

The deaths in South Waziristan are likely to fuel fresh debate in Pakistan’s parliament, where lawmakers have already demanded that the government enforce the resolution against foreign incursions more forcefully. Opposition figures are expected to call for diplomatic protests, a review of security cooperation and stronger measures to prevent future drone attacks.

As violence continues in the tribal areas, the confrontation over drone strikes underscores the fragile balance at the heart of Pakistan’s counterterrorism policy: fighting militants who threaten the state while resisting foreign military actions that many Pakistanis view as an unacceptable breach of sovereignty.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

**Pakistan protests U.S. drone strikes as violence hits northwest**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — Pakistan has lodged a formal protest with the United States over unmanned drone strikes inside Pakistani territory, saying the attacks violate the country’s sovereignty and risk undermining cooperation against militancy, Pakistani officials said.

The protest comes amid renewed tension between Islamabad and Washington over the use of U.S. drones to target suspected militants in Pakistan’s tribal regions near the Afghan border. Pakistan has repeatedly condemned the strikes publicly, calling them counterproductive and a breach of international norms, even as U.S. officials have described militants operating from the area as a direct threat to American and NATO forces in neighboring Afghanistan.

Pakistani officials said the strikes fuel anti-American sentiment and complicate the government’s efforts to confront extremist groups at home. “Such attacks are unacceptable and constitute a violation of Pakistan’s sovereignty,” a government official said, echoing language Islamabad has used in previous diplomatic complaints.

U.S. and NATO commanders have long expressed frustration that insurgent networks use sanctuaries in Pakistan’s border areas to plan and launch attacks across the frontier into Afghanistan. Washington has pressed Pakistan to take stronger action against militants, particularly in the tribal belt, where government control has historically been limited.

Pakistani leaders have rejected accusations that they are not doing enough, pointing to military operations and heavy casualties among security forces and civilians. They argue that unilateral U.S. strikes make their campaign harder by inflaming public anger and strengthening militant propaganda.

Separately, violence continued in Pakistan’s northwest.

In Mohmand Agency, part of the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas near the Afghan border, militants attacked security targets, officials said. The area has seen repeated clashes between Pakistani forces and insurgent groups, including factions of the Pakistani Taliban.

In Bannu, a city in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province that has often served as a gateway to the tribal regions, an attack also targeted security personnel, local authorities said. Details on casualties were not immediately clear.

The incidents underscored the multiple security pressures facing Pakistan: cross-border militant activity tied to the war in Afghanistan, domestic insurgent violence, and a strained partnership with the United States over counterterrorism tactics.

counterfactuals.output:
**ISLAMABAD —** Pakistan summoned U.S. Ambassador Anne Patterson on Friday to lodge a formal protest over suspected American drone strikes in the country’s northwest, as tensions between Islamabad and Washington escalated over cross-border counterterrorism operations.

Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said it had conveyed “serious concern” to the U.S. envoy, calling the missile attacks a violation of Pakistan’s sovereignty and warning that such strikes risked undermining public support for joint efforts against militancy. Officials said Islamabad demanded an immediate halt to unilateral action on Pakistani territory.

The protest followed reports of suspected U.S. drone attacks in the tribal belt along the Afghan border, an area long described by U.S. and Afghan officials as a refuge for al-Qaida and Taliban-linked militants. Pakistani officials have frequently condemned such strikes publicly, arguing that civilian casualties and the perception of foreign intrusion fuel anti-American sentiment and strengthen militant recruitment.

A Foreign Ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said Patterson was told that Pakistan “cannot accept” attacks carried out without its consent. The ministry also reiterated that counterterrorism cooperation should respect Pakistan’s territorial integrity.

The diplomatic move came amid a wave of insecurity in northwest Pakistan. Security officials reported clashes between militants and Pakistani forces in parts of the tribal areas and the North West Frontier Province, while authorities tightened security around government buildings and military installations. In recent days, the region has seen bombings, ambushes and raids targeting security personnel, underscoring the pressure on Pakistan’s government as it confronts insurgent groups near the Afghan frontier.

Washington has not officially acknowledged carrying out drone strikes inside Pakistan, but U.S. officials have long viewed the border region as central to the fight against militant networks operating in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The United States has pressed Islamabad to do more to deny safe haven to insurgents, while Pakistani leaders say their forces are already paying a heavy price in the campaign against extremism.

The latest protest highlights the uneasy nature of the U.S.-Pakistan alliance: both countries describe each other as essential partners against militancy, yet drone strikes and civilian casualties remain a recurring source of anger in Pakistan’s parliament, media and streets.

Analysts in Islamabad said the summoning of Patterson was intended both as a message to Washington and as a signal to Pakistan’s domestic audience that the government was defending national sovereignty.

“Pakistan is trying to balance cooperation with the United States against rising public anger over these strikes,” one Islamabad-based security analyst said. “Every reported drone attack makes that balance harder to maintain.”

There was no immediate comment from the U.S. Embassy on the Pakistani protest.
